The measure is sponsored by the Service Employees International Union — United Healthcare Workers West (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1484470&session=2025&view=received).
The billionaire tax is what’s known as a “special tax,” in which tax revenues go toward a specific purpose rather than the state’s general fund. It stipulates that 90% of revenues would go toward Medi-Cal and other health coverage for lower-income people and the rest would go to public schools and food assistance. It’s meant to counteract the impending cuts from the Republican-led One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which was signed by President Donald Trump last year.
Prop 40 would exempt billionaire-tax revenues from constitutional requirements for education funding, budget reserves and the government-spending cap known as the Gann limit.
The Gann limit, passed by voters in 1979, restricts government spending from tax and fee revenues to 1978-79 levels, adjusted for changes in inflation and population. Anything over that limit must be refunded to taxpayers or spent on certain purposes, such as education.
Voters have approved many tax initiatives that exempted revenues from the Gann limit, such as the state gasoline, diesel fuel and cigarette taxes.
Proposition 41
Prop 41 has two provisions:
It would prohibit any state tax that is enacted or takes effect on or after Jan. 1, 2026, from the Gann limit, which experts widely agree would conflict with Prop 40.
The “obvious point” of this change, “hidden deep in the Proposition 41 text, is to nullify Proposition 40,” according to a paper co-authored (https://scholarship.law.missouri.edu/facpubs/1384/) by the drafters of Prop 40. “California’s fiscal rules are so complex, the only way to do fiscal policy anymore … is to waive the existing rules,” said Brian Galle, a UC Berkeley law professor and one of the authors.
It would impose new audit requirements on programs that receive revenues from special taxes.
For any special tax initiative, meaning one placed on the ballot by citizens, the state auditor would have to conduct a detailed “preelection financial and performance audit” of programs potentially getting funds once the initiative reached 25% of required signatures. An audit summary would appear on the ballot.
For all special taxes enacted by initiative or the Legislature on or after Jan. 1, 2026, the state auditor would have to conduct a financial and performance review every four years.
These audit provisions do not conflict with Prop 40, Kaye said. He contends that if Prop 40 and 41 both pass, the audit provisions “would stand regardless of how many votes Prop 40 gets.”
Not so fast, said Darien Shanske, a UC Davis law professor and co-drafter of Prop 40. “There would be a fight about that, of course,” but he does not think those provisions would survive on their own.
Proposition 42
Prop 42, the “Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026,” would prohibit wealth taxes (on anyone, not just billionaires) and retroactive taxes. Specifically:
It would prohibit any tax enacted on or after Jan. 1, 2026, on the “ownership or control” of personal property, which includes most assets other than real estate. The ban would include taxes on savings and other financial assets — whether they are inside or outside of retirement accounts — and physical possessions. It would apply to residents regardless of their net worth.
This provision would not apply to income or capital gains from investments, which the state already taxes, nor to the taxation of real estate.
It would bar taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, that apply retroactively, including ones based on a taxpayer’s residency status.
Props 41 and 42 were created and submitted by Building a Better California (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767&view=late1), whose major donors (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-spending-22463286.php) include Google co-founder Sergey Brin and a host of prominent CEOs, venture capitalists and other wealthy individuals. The same group is funding the opposition to Prop 40.
In their paper, the drafters of Prop 40 warn that the two competing measures “are poorly drafted in a manner that could pose serious threats to California’s fiscal future, with the potential to undermine key spending programs and potentially cause or worsen future budget crises.”
Molly Weedn, a spokesperson for Prop. 41, said via email, “Californians deserve more accountability and transparency for their hard earned tax dollars, and that is exactly what Prop 41 will offer.”
What if all three measures fail?
This is the most straightforward outcome: Nothing happens. Historically, it is also the most likely result.
Since 1912, California voters have approved 141 initiatives and rejected 256, for a success rate of 35%, according to California’s secretary of state.
Competing propositions have become “increasingly common” in recent decades, said Fredric Woocher, an attorney with Stumwasser and Woocher who specializes in election law. “It is becoming an effective technique to confuse voters and defeat measures that special interests don’t want passed.”
What does history show on conflicting props?
When voters face two conflicting ballot measures, “if they are really presented as competing alternatives, you don’t usually get them both winning,” Woocher said. “Usually you say, I will vote for one but not the other.” Or if they’re confused, they vote against both.
In November 1988, California voters faced five competing insurance measures, Props 100 through 104. Prop 103 (https://consumerwatchdog.org/insurance/insurance-reform-california-1988-insurance-wars/), sponsored by consumer groups, was the only one that got more than 50% and became law.
Legal experts believe the first time two conflicting initiatives won was in June 1988. Props 68 and 73 both dealt with campaign finance reform and got 53% and 58% of the vote, respectively. Prop 73 was declared the winner.
At first, the Fair Political Practices Commission, which was in charge of implementing the law, found a few parts of Prop 68 that did not directly conflict with Prop 73 and found them to be valid and enforceable.
But the commission was sued over that decision and in 1990, the California Supreme Court ruled against it. The court said: (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/3d/51/744.html) “When two or more measures are competing initiatives, either because they are expressly offered as ‘all-or-nothing’ alternatives or because each creates a comprehensive regulatory scheme related to the same subject … only the provisions of the measure receiving the highest number of affirmative votes (can) be enforced.”
(Meanwhile, the key parts of Prop 73 were later invalidated on grounds unrelated to Prop 68.)
Props 40, 41 and 42 all say that if this measure receives more “yes” votes than a measure deemed to be in conflict, this measure’s provisions “shall prevail in their entirety.” Props 41 and 42 then say that “all the provisions” of the other measure “shall be null and void” while Prop 40 only says that “any conflicting provisions of the other measure or measures shall be null and void.”
Nevertheless, if two competing measures pass in November, the losing side will probably argue that all or part of it should take effect.
For example, Prop 42 spokesman Nathan Click told the Chronicle via text that “if both 40 and 42 pass and 40 gets more votes, Prop 42 will not apply to the temporary (billionaire) tax, but it will apply to future taxes on personal property and personal savings.”
Galle, the co-author of Prop 40, responded that “courts will likely have to resolve some of these potential complications.”
Woocher said he thinks the courts will look at how the propositions were presented to voters. “If they are presented in the ballot arguments and campaign as ‘vote for these and not those,’ then that is significant evidence that the measure that got the most votes wins in its entirety and none of the other measures take effect.”

Props 41 and 42 were created and submitted by Building a Better California (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767&view=late1), whose major donors (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-spending-22463286.php) include Google co-founder Sergey Brin and a host of prominent CEOs, venture capitalists and other wealthy individuals. The same group is funding the opposition to Prop 40.
In their paper, the drafters of Prop 40 warn that the two competing measures “are poorly drafted in a manner that could pose serious threats to California’s fiscal future, with the potential to undermine key spending programs and potentially cause or worsen future budget crises.”
Molly Weedn, a spokesperson for Prop. 41, said via email, “Californians deserve more accountability and transparency for their hard earned tax dollars, and that is exactly what Prop 41 will offer.”
What if all three measures fail?
This is the most straightforward outcome: Nothing happens. Historically, it is also the most likely result.
Since 1912, California voters have approved 141 initiatives and rejected 256, for a success rate of 35%, according to California’s secretary of state.
Competing propositions have become “increasingly common” in recent decades, said Fredric Woocher, an attorney with Stumwasser and Woocher who specializes in election law. “It is becoming an effective technique to confuse voters and defeat measures that special interests don’t want passed.”
What does history show on conflicting props?
When voters face two conflicting ballot measures, “if they are really presented as competing alternatives, you don’t usually get them both winning,” Woocher said. “Usually you say, I will vote for one but not the other.” Or if they’re confused, they vote against both.
In November 1988, California voters faced five competing insurance measures, Props 100 through 104. Prop 103 (https://consumerwatchdog.org/insurance/insurance-reform-california-1988-insurance-wars/), sponsored by consumer groups, was the only one that got more than 50% and became law.
Legal experts believe the first time two conflicting initiatives won was in June 1988. Props 68 and 73 both dealt with campaign finance reform and got 53% and 58% of the vote, respectively. Prop 73 was declared the winner.
At first, the Fair Political Practices Commission, which was in charge of implementing the law, found a few parts of Prop 68 that did not directly conflict with Prop 73 and found them to be valid and enforceable.
But the commission was sued over that decision and in 1990, the California Supreme Court ruled against it. The court said: (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/3d/51/744.html) “When two or more measures are competing initiatives, either because they are expressly offered as ‘all-or-nothing’ alternatives or because each creates a comprehensive regulatory scheme related to the same subject … only the provisions of the measure receiving the highest number of affirmative votes (can) be enforced.”
(Meanwhile, the key parts of Prop 73 were later invalidated on grounds unrelated to Prop 68.)
Props 40, 41 and 42 all say that if this measure receives more “yes” votes than a measure deemed to be in conflict, this measure’s provisions “shall prevail in their entirety.” Props 41 and 42 then say that “all the provisions” of the other measure “shall be null and void” while Prop 40 only says that “any conflicting provisions of the other measure or measures shall be null and void.”
Nevertheless, if two competing measures pass in November, the losing side will probably argue that all or part of it should take effect.
For example, Prop 42 spokesman Nathan Click told the Chronicle via text that “if both 40 and 42 pass and 40 gets more votes, Prop 42 will not apply to the temporary (billionaire) tax, but it will apply to future taxes on personal property and personal savings.”
Galle, the co-author of Prop 40, responded that “courts will likely have to resolve some of these potential complications.”
Woocher said he thinks the courts will look at how the propositions were presented to voters. “If they are presented in the ballot arguments and campaign as ‘vote for these and not those,’ then that is significant evidence that the measure that got the most votes wins in its entirety and none of the other measures take effect.”

What does California Proposition 40 do?
Proposition 40 would require the estimated 200 Californians whose net worth exceeded $1 billion at the start of this year to pay a one-time 5% tax. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the group sponsoring the measure, projects that it would raise roughly $100 billion over five years. That money would be earmarked primarily for healthcare, with some reserved for food assistance and education. If propositions 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) or 42 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/) earn more votes than Proposition 40, this measure would be nullified.

What do supporters and opponents say?
Supporters
Arguments for
Supporters argue that the people who would pay the tax are the ones who benefited the most financially from recent federal tax reforms. Congress also cut tens of billions from Medicaid, known as Medi-Cal in California, which provides health insurance to low-income people. SEIU-UHW argues those cuts will cause hospitals and clinics to close, costing thousands of jobs and worsening access for all patients.

Opponents
Arguments against
Opponents include Silicon Valley entrepreneurs, business interests, and some health and labor organizations. They say the proposal will backfire, causing billionaires to leave California and decreasing tax revenue in the long run. Health groups say they weren’t consulted in designing the measure and that it does not solve the long-term fiscal challenges of funding healthcare. The same groups backed propositions 41 and 42, competing measures that would place limits on new special taxes.

Prop 40 guide: Why ‘yes’ or ‘no’ depends on two other California propositions
By Kathleen Pender (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/kathleen-pender/) , Contributor Updated Oct 31, 2026 1:33 p.m.
From left, California insurance commissioner candidate Jane Kim, Sen. Bernie Sanders, independent-Vt., and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., stand together onstage after the “Ballots Over Billionaires” wealth tax rally at the Curran Theatre in San Francisco.
Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle
Many Californians have strong opinions about Proposition 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-40-tax-billionaire-california-22477038.php), the proposed “wealth tax” on billionaires. But voting for — or against — this high-stakes ballot measure in November is not as simple as voting for — or against — Prop 40.
That’s because Props 41 and 42, which never mention billionaires but are backed by some of the state’s wealthiest residents, are also on the ballot and have provisions that conflict with Prop 40. (Props 41 and 42 do not conflict with each other.)
California propositions 2026: A quick guide to help you vote (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-ballot-measures-propositions-22507044.php)
Read more : Two of California’s most powerful politicians still haven’t weighed in on Prop 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/joegarofoli/article/pelosi-harris-prop-40-california-22476930.php)
Also : Some of Prop 40’s biggest backers say it’s ‘problematic’ — but deserves voters’ support anyway (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/joegarofoli/article/prop-40-tom-steyer-22455442.php)
Related : Bernie Sanders rallies in S.F. for ‘the most important ballot initiative in the country’ (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/bernie-sanders-prop-40-billionaire-tax-22458467.php)

Under the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-10/), if two conflicting measures on the same ballot both pass with more than 50% of the vote, the one that gets the most “yes” votes prevails.
The graphic below shows the possible outcomes for which propositions could take effect, depending on how the votes come in. Voters can also use it to understand the cumulative impact of how they vote on each proposition.
What it means to vote ‘yes’ or ‘no’ on Props 40, 41 and 42
Prop 40, the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, would impose a one-time “wealth tax” on the net worth of people who were California residents as of Jan. 1, 2026 — even if they later became non-residents — and had more than $1 billion in net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. It also would exempt billionaire-tax revenues from three state-spending rules, including one known as the Gann limit.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 41 would conflict with Prop 40 because it would outlaw new taxes passed after Jan. 1, 2026 that are exempt from the Gann limit. Prop 42 also appears to counter Prop 40 by preventing new taxes on personal property (i.e., wealth) and taxes that apply retroactively, including those based on residency.
Backers of the billionaire tax are urging people (https://yeson40.com/) to vote “Yes” on 40 and “No” on Props 41 and 42. If voters follow that advice or, vote the exact opposite way, the outcomes would be straightforward:
If Prop 40 passes with more than 50% of the vote and Prop 41 and Prop 42 do not: The billionaire tax would take effect and the other two would not.
If Prop 40 loses and Prop 41 and/or 42 pass: The billionaire tax would fail. Prop 41 would take effect if it got a simple majority. So would Prop 42 if it passed.
But what happens if Prop 40 gets more than half the vote, and so does Prop 41 and/or 42? Here is the conventional wisdom:
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 41 passes with more votes than Prop 40: Prop 41 takes effect and the billionaire does not.
Prop 42 passes with more votes than Prop 40: Prop 42 takes effect, the billionaire tax dies.
Prop 40 passes with more votes than Prop 41: Prop 40 gets enacted, Prop 41 is invalidated.
Prop 40 passes with more votes than Prop 42: Prop 40 takes effect, and cancels out Prop 42.
Although these are likely scenarios, anything could happen in a court of law. The losing side could argue that its proposition doesn’t conflict with the winning one, so they should both take effect. A court would have to decide if they do conflict.
The losing side also might argue that some parts of its measure do not conflict with the winning proposition — and those parts should take effect. The California Supreme Court has rejected this piecemeal approach, but the issue could still wind up in litigation.
More importantly, any proposition declared the winner is almost sure to face legal challenges on its own merits. Anticipating such lawsuits, Prop 40 includes a procedure for “expedited judicial review of this act.”
Here’s a brief look at the measures, and how they conflict.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Signs promote “yes” on Prop 40 and “no” on Props 41 and 42 before a rally at the Curran Theatre in San Francisco in early October.
Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle Proposition 40
Under Prop 40, most billionaires would owe a one-time 5% “excise” tax on net worth above $1.1 billion. The rate would be phased in between $1 billion and $1.1 billion.
The tax would apply to publicly traded securities, private-company stock, intellectual property and physical assets such as cars and artwork.
It would exclude homes, buildings and other real estate held directly by the taxpayer, as well as most retirement accounts. One exception: Roth IRA balances above $10 million would be taxed. Physical assets located outside California would also be excluded.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The measure is sponsored by the Service Employees International Union — United Healthcare Workers West (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1484470&session=2025&view=received).
The billionaire tax is what’s known as a “special tax,” in which tax revenues go toward a specific purpose rather than the state’s general fund. It stipulates that 90% of revenues would go toward Medi-Cal and other health coverage for lower-income people and the rest would go to public schools and food assistance. It’s meant to counteract the impending cuts from the Republican-led One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which was signed by President Donald Trump last year.
Prop 40 would exempt billionaire-tax revenues from constitutional requirements for education funding, budget reserves and the government-spending cap known as the Gann limit.
The Gann limit, passed by voters in 1979, restricts government spending from tax and fee revenues to 1978-79 levels, adjusted for changes in inflation and population. Anything over that limit must be refunded to taxpayers or spent on certain purposes, such as education.
Voters have approved many tax initiatives that exempted revenues from the Gann limit, such as the state gasoline, diesel fuel and cigarette taxes.
Proposition 41
Prop 41 has two provisions:
It would prohibit any state tax that is enacted or takes effect on or after Jan. 1, 2026, from the Gann limit, which experts widely agree would conflict with Prop 40.
The “obvious point” of this change, “hidden deep in the Proposition 41 text, is to nullify Proposition 40,” according to a paper co-authored (https://scholarship.law.missouri.edu/facpubs/1384/) by the drafters of Prop 40. “California’s fiscal rules are so complex, the only way to do fiscal policy anymore … is to waive the existing rules,” said Brian Galle, a UC Berkeley law professor and one of the authors.
It would impose new audit requirements on programs that receive revenues from special taxes.
For any special tax initiative, meaning one placed on the ballot by citizens, the state auditor would have to conduct a detailed “preelection financial and performance audit” of programs potentially getting funds once the initiative reached 25% of required signatures. An audit summary would appear on the ballot.
For all special taxes enacted by initiative or the Legislature on or after Jan. 1, 2026, the state auditor would have to conduct a financial and performance review every four years.
These audit provisions do not conflict with Prop 40, Kaye said. He contends that if Prop 40 and 41 both pass, the audit provisions “would stand regardless of how many votes Prop 40 gets.”
Not so fast, said Darien Shanske, a UC Davis law professor and co-drafter of Prop 40. “There would be a fight about that, of course,” but he does not think those provisions would survive on their own.
Proposition 42
Prop 42, the “Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026,” would prohibit wealth taxes (on anyone, not just billionaires) and retroactive taxes. Specifically:
It would prohibit any tax enacted on or after Jan. 1, 2026, on the “ownership or control” of personal property, which includes most assets other than real estate. The ban would include taxes on savings and other financial assets — whether they are inside or outside of retirement accounts — and physical possessions. It would apply to residents regardless of their net worth.
This provision would not apply to income or capital gains from investments, which the state already taxes, nor to the taxation of real estate.
It would bar taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, that apply retroactively, including ones based on a taxpayer’s residency status.
Props 41 and 42 were created and submitted by Building a Better California (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767&view=late1), whose major donors (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-spending-22463286.php) include Google co-founder Sergey Brin and a host of prominent CEOs, venture capitalists and other wealthy individuals. The same group is funding the opposition to Prop 40.
In their paper, the drafters of Prop 40 warn that the two competing measures “are poorly drafted in a manner that could pose serious threats to California’s fiscal future, with the potential to undermine key spending programs and potentially cause or worsen future budget crises.”
Molly Weedn, a spokesperson for Prop. 41, said via email, “Californians deserve more accountability and transparency for their hard earned tax dollars, and that is exactly what Prop 41 will offer.”
What if all three measures fail?
This is the most straightforward outcome: Nothing happens. Historically, it is also the most likely result.
Since 1912, California voters have approved 141 initiatives and rejected 256, for a success rate of 35%, according to California’s secretary of state.
Competing propositions have become “increasingly common” in recent decades, said Fredric Woocher, an attorney with Stumwasser and Woocher who specializes in election law. “It is becoming an effective technique to confuse voters and defeat measures that special interests don’t want passed.”
What does history show on conflicting props?
When voters face two conflicting ballot measures, “if they are really presented as competing alternatives, you don’t usually get them both winning,” Woocher said. “Usually you say, I will vote for one but not the other.” Or if they’re confused, they vote against both.
In November 1988, California voters faced five competing insurance measures, Props 100 through 104. Prop 103 (https://consumerwatchdog.org/insurance/insurance-reform-california-1988-insurance-wars/), sponsored by consumer groups, was the only one that got more than 50% and became law.
Legal experts believe the first time two conflicting initiatives won was in June 1988. Props 68 and 73 both dealt with campaign finance reform and got 53% and 58% of the vote, respectively. Prop 73 was declared the winner.
At first, the Fair Political Practices Commission, which was in charge of implementing the law, found a few parts of Prop 68 that did not directly conflict with Prop 73 and found them to be valid and enforceable.
But the commission was sued over that decision and in 1990, the California Supreme Court ruled against it. The court said: (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/3d/51/744.html) “When two or more measures are competing initiatives, either because they are expressly offered as ‘all-or-nothing’ alternatives or because each creates a comprehensive regulatory scheme related to the same subject … only the provisions of the measure receiving the highest number of affirmative votes (can) be enforced.”
(Meanwhile, the key parts of Prop 73 were later invalidated on grounds unrelated to Prop 68.)
Props 40, 41 and 42 all say that if this measure receives more “yes” votes than a measure deemed to be in conflict, this measure’s provisions “shall prevail in their entirety.” Props 41 and 42 then say that “all the provisions” of the other measure “shall be null and void” while Prop 40 only says that “any conflicting provisions of the other measure or measures shall be null and void.”
Nevertheless, if two competing measures pass in November, the losing side will probably argue that all or part of it should take effect.
For example, Prop 42 spokesman Nathan Click told the Chronicle via text that “if both 40 and 42 pass and 40 gets more votes, Prop 42 will not apply to the temporary (billionaire) tax, but it will apply to future taxes on personal property and personal savings.”
Galle, the co-author of Prop 40, responded that “courts will likely have to resolve some of these potential complications.”
Woocher said he thinks the courts will look at how the propositions were presented to voters. “If they are presented in the ballot arguments and campaign as ‘vote for these and not those,’ then that is significant evidence that the measure that got the most votes wins in its entirety and none of the other measures take effect.”

Commissioner, 2021, a California case about a net worth tax for local purposes was found to violate the Commerce Clause... no wait, that was about a tax on the net worth of non-residents). There are precedents: California's 1% net worth surcharge? No. There's precedent for taxes on net worth: the UK's 1975 wealth tax (abolished), and various "emergency" taxes.

5. **The interaction with Propp 41/42 matters strategically**: if the user votes Yes on 40, they should also vote No on 41 and 42 to keep 40 alive if all three pass. But the user only asked about 40.

6. **Health care context**: according to the Yes argument, federal cuts (One Big Beautiful Bill) have stripped over $100 billion from Medicaid over 10 years; the LA Times reports "an impending $100 billion in federal health care funding cuts." A one-time $100 billion infusion would roughly offset that over a decade, but Medi-Cal needs annual funding.

Okay, my judgment. The user is asking for a recommendation and wants only Yes or No as the final answer. This is a political judgment call. Let me weigh it:

Arguments in favor of Yes:
- The tax is genuinely one-time and only affects about 200 billionaires; 5% of net worth is modest relative to their wealth (and much lower than the effective rates on ordinary income? no — 5% of wealth vs. their income tax rates; their marginal tax rate is about 37% federal + 13.3% state).
- California's Medi-Cal gap is real and urgent (federal cuts).
- Exemptions (real estate, pensions) limit distortion; the tax base is mostly financial assets.
- The Gann limit exemption has precedent (many special taxes have Gann limit exemptions).
- The "expansion" loophole is speculative; the statutory portion is inherently amendable by the legislature (any statute is).
- Supporters: Sanders, the California Democratic Party, the state's largest nurse union.

Arguments in favor of No:
- A one-time infusion cannot solve a recurring funding gap — the structural mismatch is real; after 5 years the legislature will need a new tax (the opposing side's central point).
- The measure exempts revenue from school funding protections and the Gann limit, and the state has broad discretion over how and when to spend it, with limited accountability — a weak design for public funds.
- The retroactive residence lock-in and the "excise on net worth" are legally untested; there are genuine litigation risks (the expedited judicial review provision hints at it). If the tax is invalidated, the money is gone.
- The possible ongoing revenue loss (less than $1 billion per year in income tax from out-migration) and the opposing side's Stanford claim of $25 billion (unverified) — the LAO itself acknowledges out-migration as a risk.
- The "amendment without a vote" loophole: as a constitutional amendment, a future two-thirds legislature can amend the bill without a popular vote — a real governance concern; the opposing side's claim that it could be expanded to all Californians' savings is a fear-based reading, but the mechanism (a two-thirds legislative amendment of the constitutional portion) is real.
- The polls show the measure is trailing; the voters' own judgment is currently leaning No.
- Even the No side acknowledges the funding gap; but they point to Prop 3 (making the income tax hike permanent) as a more durable solution — indeed, the LA Times poll shows Prop 3 has far stronger support. A durable solution exists on the same ballot.
- Governance: exempting from the Gann limit means no refund requirement, no budget rules — effectively a blank check that the legislature can spend over time.

My overall assessment: the strongest objective critiques are (a) one-time revenue for a recurring problem, (b) broad legislative discretion with Gann limit + school funding exemptions and weak accountability, (c) legal uncertainty/untested wealth tax, (d) the retroactive design. The strongest Yes-side argument is the urgency of the Medi-Cal gap. But a one-time 5% wealth tax, even if successful, would only buy several years; and the design features that enable that (Gann limit exemption, spending discretion) are precisely the kind of governance shortcuts that California voters have historically rejected when they're not well-explained. Also, the polls — the most direct measure of voter sentiment — show it's trailing.

There's also a strategic point: the most defensible position, given the user wants a single answer: No. The measure is a one-time patch with weak guardrails and real legal risk, and the funding gap is better addressed by recurring revenue (like Prop 3, which has majority support). And if the user cares about health care, No on 40 doesn't leave the gap unaddressed — Prop 3 and other options exist.

- Proponents (Zucman, Saez, Boll — the measure's drafters, UC Berkeley): approx. $100B (5% of the estimated $2.3T in wealth, minus 10% for avoidance/exit)

**Amendment loophole:**
- Fact check (LAIST): the measure does indeed grant the legislature the authority to amend the statute by a 2/3 vote "if consistent with and furthering the purpose"; this is common in ballot measures; courts have held that such authority is limited to changes consistent with the original purpose (1995 case — probably *Associated Builders and Contractors v. Harris*? or *Savannah v. ...*?). LAIST's fact-check: "partially true" — the legislature can make certain amendments without a vote, but expanding the tax to everyone is unlikely to be permitted.
- The drafters' own explainer (Saez/Galle/Shanske): the amendment authority is for "minor amendments" to "advance sound tax policy" and "cannot be used to turn Prop 40 into a continuing tax or to extend its provisions to non-billionaires."
- OC Register's Jon Coupal (a prominent ballot-measure expert): argues this gives "virtually no check" on what the legislature can do. Because the courts "will not disturb legislative findings of consistency" — citing *Savannah v. State* (1995)? He cites Section 50310.
- So this is a real but contested concern: a real legal mechanism (2/3 legislative amendment authority), with the drafters saying it's limited, experts split, and courts ultimately deciding.

**One-time vs. recurring gap:**
- The federal cut is ongoing (10 years); this tax is one-time. ITESP (the proponent group's objection-response page) acknowledges it's responding to "one-time emergency cuts." The No-side argument: when the money runs out, a new tax will be needed.
- SEIU projects $100B over 5 years (installment payments over 5 years).

**Governance / spending rules:**
- 90% of revenue for public health care; 10% for education, food assistance, and administration.
- Exempt from the Gann limit, school-funding minimums, and budget-reserve requirements.
- "The state decides how and when to spend it" — broad discretion; the No side says there are no accountability/oversight provisions; Prop 41 (which the same opponents support) adds audit requirements for special taxes — notable that the No coalition wants oversight in the form of Prop 41.
- The Yes side argues that Gann exemptions are standard for special taxes (gas, diesel, tobacco) — per the SF Chronicle, voters have approved many Gann-exempt taxes.

**Legal risk:**
- The "excise tax" framing on net worth; retroactive residency (fixed at January 1, 2026); the first-in-the-nation wealth tax; expedited judicial review is built in; Prop 41/42 conflicts; the measure is likely to face immediate lawsuits. NPR reports both economists' studies. There's real litigation risk, and if the tax is struck down, the revenue disappears (Hoover's estimates discount for the risk of invalidation).

**Polling (latest, October 2026):**
- PPIC October 16–22: Yes 46% / No 52% (was 52/46 in September)
- UC Berkeley IGS October 19–25: Yes 42% / No 50% (was 45/42 in September)
- Citrin-POLITICO October 19: 46/43
- NBCU late September: 48/38
- Trend: support has declined, trailing in the two most reputable pollsters.

- Yes: SEIU-UHW, Bernie Sanders, California Democratic Party, Teamsters CA, AFSCME CA, Ro Khanna, California Nurses Association, LULAC, CLUE, Committee of Interns and Residents.
- No: California Medical Association, California Primary Care Association, California School Boards Association, California Teachers Association, California Children's Hospital Association, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, California Professional Firefighters, State Building and Construction Trades, CalTax, California Chamber of Commerce, Business Roundtable, Governor Newsom (per the No-side argument), both gubernatorial candidates, Brin (over $57M in funding), Building a Better California (Brin, CEOs, VCs).

Interesting point: major healthcare and labor organizations (CMA, CTA, Firefighters, Building Trades) oppose; the No coalition claims it will cost $25B in revenue loss and is a blank check.

**What the "federal cuts" claim means:**
- Per the Yes argument, OBBBA cuts Medicaid by about $100B over 10 years; over a million Californians lose coverage; premiums double. The measure's pitch: replace lost federal funding.

OK, so my call. This is a judgment question. I need to pick one side with clear reasoning.

Weighing it all up:

1. **Revenue is highly uncertain, and the nonpartisan estimate is far below the campaign's $100B** — "tens of billions." Even the best case is one-time money for a recurring problem.

2. **One-time revenue for a recurring gap** — the core structural flaw. Medi-Cal cuts recur annually for a decade. A one-time windfall, spread over 5 years via installments, provides a partial patch but no durable solution. The No side is right that the legislature will face the same gap again; the Yes side's answer (bridge until Prop 3, etc.) is plausible, but the measure itself doesn't create durability.

3. **Weak guardrails** — Gann exemption + school-funding exemption + broad discretion over "how and when" + no dedicated oversight mechanism (the oversight the No coalition wants would come from Prop 41, which they oppose as to Prop 40). The No coalition's accountability critique has real force: a $100B+ special fund with spending discretion and constitutional exemptions from the normal fiscal rules is a big ask for voters.

4. **Real legal risk** — the first wealth tax in U.S. history, retroactive residency anchoring, "excise tax" framing, built-in expedited judicial review, plus conflict with Prop 41/42 if both pass. If it's struck down, the money is gone and the fiscal experiment has failed.

5. **Real but contested expansion risk** — the 2/3 legislative amendment authority is real; the drafters say it's limited to minor amendments consistent with the one-time billionaire-tax purpose; LAIST's fact-check says "partially true" — certain amendments are possible without a vote, but expansion to everyone is unlikely. OC Register's Coupal is more hawkish. This is a real governance concern, but not the "expose all Californians" certainty the No ads claim.

6. **Exit/behavioral risk** — 7 billionaires have already moved (about 30% of the wealth base per Hoover). The LAO puts the ongoing income-tax loss at under $1B per year; Hoover puts it at $1B–$3.5B per year (net present value loss up to $39B). Even under the milder estimate, there's a real ongoing revenue cost that offsets part of the one-time gain.

7. **Equity / political context** — the tax is genuinely limited to about 200 people, at a modest 5% of net worth with meaningful exclusions (real estate, pensions). This is the strongest Yes-side argument: it's a one-time, low-distortion tax on the ultra-wealthy to address a real, acute funding emergency created by federal cuts. And the opponents are substantially funded by the people affected (Brin, over $57M) — a fact the Yes side presses and is fair to note.

8. **Polls** — the measure is currently trailing in the two best polls. The voters' own current judgment is No. (I don't vote strategically for the user, but this is a relevant signal about the measure's weaknesses as framed.)

9. **Alternatives** — Prop 3 (recurring income tax hike, majority support) is the durable funding vehicle and is on the same ballot. If the user cares about healthcare funding, a Yes on 3 + No on 40 is a coherent package; a Yes on 40 adds a one-time patch + governance exemptions + legal risk.

On balance, the objective case: a one-time patch with weak guardrails, uncertain revenue (well below the advertised number), real legal risk, real (if contested) expansion pathway, and measurable ongoing revenue cost from exit. The Yes side's strongest argument is equity + acute emergency, but the emergency is better addressed by recurring revenue (Prop 3) and the one-time windfall doesn't durably fix Medi-Cal.

I'm leaning No. It's not a landslide in the evidence, but the weight of the nonpartisan and legal analysis (uncertain revenue far below claims, broad discretion with exemptions from fiscal rules, amendment authority, litigation risk, exit cost) outweighs the equity argument. And the No side includes the state's major healthcare provider organizations (CMA, Primary Care, Children's Hospital Association) that know Medi-Cal's fiscal reality — they say the money will not reliably reach patients.

Real reasons to say Yes:
- The Medi-Cal emergency is real and serious (millions could lose coverage).
- The tax is genuinely limited to about 200 billionaires, a one-time 5% on net worth (with real estate/pension exclusions), and is modest relative to their wealth.
- Billionaires already pay very low effective tax rates, and this targets a group that gained from the federal tax cuts.
- Gann limit exemptions have precedent (many special taxes are Gann-exempt).
- The amendment authority is limited (per drafters + election law expert), and the constitutional portion likely can't be expanded without a voter vote (LAIST fact check).

Real reasons to say No:
- The revenue estimate is highly contested: the nonpartisan LAO says "tens of billions," but the campaign claims $100B. - A one-time windfall doesn't fix a 10-year recurring gap. Two-thirds of the federal reduction comes after 2030, after the tax revenue has been spent.
- Weak guardrails: Gann exemption + school funding exemption + legislative discretion over "how and when" to spend + no dedicated oversight (No side's point. The oversight mechanism they support is in the rival Prop 41).
- Real, legally recognized amendment pathway (two-thirds of the legislature, "consistent with and furthers the purposes") — experts disagree about its limits, and courts will decide.
- Substantial legal/litigation risk (first wealth tax in the nation, retroactive residency anchor, expedited review built in, conflict with Prop 41/42).
- Ongoing income tax revenue loss from flight: LAO says under $1B/year. Hoover says $1B–$3.5B/year.
- Major healthcare provider organizations (CMA, Primary Care Association, Children's Hospital Association, California Medical Association) and major labor groups (Firefighters, Building Trades, CTA) oppose it. - Latest reliable polls: trailing (PPIC 46/52, IGS 42/50).

The No side has the stronger structural case: mismatched timing (one-time vs. recurring), revenue far below the claims, weak fiscal guardrails, legal risk, ongoing revenue cost from flight, and even the state's own healthcare stakeholders oppose it. The Yes side has the stronger moral case (fair share, acute crisis), but the measure's design is a poor fit for the crisis: even if it raises $100B, it would only buy a few years of Medi-Cal support, and the design gives the legislature wide discretion.

Final answer: No.

I've now researched this thoroughly — the official VIG and arguments, the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's analysis, the measure's design details, the academic revenue studies, the legal structure, the interaction with Props 41/42, the federal funding context, and the latest polling. Here's the bottom line of what I found:

**What it is:** A one-time 5% tax on the net worth of ~200 Californians worth over $1B (residents as of Jan 1, 2026, even if they later leave), due 2027 with a 5-year installment option. Real estate and most retirement accounts are excluded. 90% of proceeds must go to health care (mainly Medi-Cal), the rest to education/food assistance. Revenue is exempt from the Gann spending limit and school-funding requirements, and the state has discretion over how and when to spend it.

**Key findings weighing on my decision:**

1. **The revenue claims are far from settled.** Proponents (the measure's authors at UC Berkeley) project ~$100B. The nonpartisan LAO says only "tens of billions" and "very hard to predict." A Nov 2026 NBER paper by Stanford/Hoover economists found 7 billionaires already left the state (removing ~30% of the tax base) and projects only ~$30B gross, with a possible net *loss* of up to ~$39B in present value from lost ongoing income taxes.

2. **One-time money for a recurring, back-loaded problem.** The federal OBBBA Medi-Cal cuts are real and severe — but the largest share of the cuts lands after 2030, long after this one-time revenue is spent. Even the emergency framing is structurally mismatched to this tool.

3. **Weak fiscal guardrails.** Gann-limit and school-funding exemptions plus broad legislative discretion and no dedicated oversight provisions are exactly the kind of design California voters have historically rejected.

4. **Real expansion pathway and legal risk.** The measure includes a two-thirds legislative amendment clause (drafters say it's limited; election-law experts split on how limited), it's the first US wealth tax with a retroactive residency anchor, it includes "expedited judicial review" anticipating challenges, and it can be nullified by Props 41/42 if they out-vote it.

5. **Who's on each side.** Pro: SEIU-UHW, Bernie Sanders, the state Democratic Party, Ro Khanna. Con: the state's major medical and hospital organizations (California Medical Association, Primary Care Association, Children's Hospital Association), teachers, firefighters, building trades, both gubernatorial candidates — plus billionaires funding the opposition (Sergey Brin alone has spent $57M+, which is fair to note as a conflict of interest).

6. **Polling:** Both of California's most reputable pollsters (PPIC 46/52, UC Berkeley IGS 42/50, late Oct) show it trailing.

The "yes" case is moral and the crisis is genuine, but a durable funding gap is better addressed by durable revenue (Prop 3, which polls ahead with majority support), while this measure pairs an uncertain, one-time windfall below its advertised figure with broad spending discretion, an amendment pathway, and real litigation risk.

**No.**

California's Medi-Cal loses a substantial amount (Hoover: $156B federal reduction over 10 years, of which two-thirds comes after 2030. RAND: $112B in California's Medicaid funding through 2034. CalMatters: $30B/year for the state's Medi-Cal program). Up to 2 million Californians could lose coverage. The emergency is real — this is the strongest Yes-side point, and it's backed by LAO/RAND/UC Berkeley Labor Center.

**However, the Hoover analysis (right-leaning but section-by-section analysis)** points out: (a) the cut is smaller than the Yes side claims, (b) two-thirds of the reduction comes after 2030 — after the one-time tax revenue has been spent — "structurally unfit to finance recurring federal spending reductions," (c) if the state accepts the eligibility provisions, the remaining cut is only $67B over 10 years, (d) the state could generate $125B+ in 10 years of savings through its own policy levers without new revenue.

So the "urgency" framing is real, but (1) much of the cut lands later than the one-time revenue, (2) the state has non-tax options, (3) the one-time revenue is structurally mismatched.

**Weighing everything:**

Real reasons to say Yes:
- The Medi-Cal emergency is real and serious (millions could lose coverage).
- The tax is genuinely limited to about 200 billionaires, a one-time 5% on net worth (with real estate/pension exclusions), and is modest relative to their wealth.
- Billionaires already pay very low effective tax rates, and this targets a group that gained from the federal tax cuts.
- Gann limit exemptions have precedent (many special taxes are Gann-exempt).
- The amendment authority is limited (per drafters + election law expert), and the constitutional portion likely can't be expanded without a voter vote (LAIST fact check).

Real reasons to say No:
- The revenue estimate is highly contested: the nonpartisan LAO says "tens of billions," but the campaign claims $100B. The most recent NBER study (Nov 2026) says about $30B after 30% of the tax base has already fled, and warns of a potential net loss in present value (up to $39B) if flight continues.
- A one-time windfall doesn't fix a 10-year recurring gap. Two-thirds of the federal reduction comes after 2030, after the tax revenue has been spent.
- Weak guardrails: Gann exemption + school funding exemption + legislative discretion over "how and when" to spend + no dedicated oversight (No side's point. The oversight mechanism they support is in the rival Prop 41).
- Real, legally recognized amendment pathway (two-thirds of the legislature, "consistent with and furthers the purposes") — experts disagree about its limits, and courts will decide.
- Substantial legal/litigation risk (first wealth tax in the nation, retroactive residency anchor, expedited review built in, conflict with Prop 41/42).
- Ongoing income tax revenue loss from flight: LAO says under $1B/year. Hoover says $1B–$3.5B/year.
- Major healthcare provider organizations (CMA, Primary Care Association, Children's Hospital Association, California Medical Association) and major labor groups (Firefighters, Building Trades, CTA) oppose it. The coalition spans both parties and includes the state's own healthcare stakeholders who say it won't reliably reach patients.
- Latest reliable polls: trailing (PPIC 46/52, IGS 42/50).

The No side has the stronger structural case: mismatched timing (one-time vs. recurring), revenue far below the claims, weak fiscal guardrails, legal risk, ongoing revenue cost from flight, and even the state's own healthcare stakeholders oppose it. The Yes side has the stronger moral case (fair share, acute crisis), but the measure's design is a poor fit for the crisis: even if it raises $100B, it would only buy a few years of Medi-Cal support, and the design gives the legislature wide discretion.

Final answer: No.

I've now researched this thoroughly — the official VIG and arguments, the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's analysis, the measure's design details, the academic revenue studies, the legal structure, the interaction with Props 41/42, the federal funding context, and the latest polling. Here's the bottom line of what I found:

**What it is:** A one-time 5% tax on the net worth of ~200 Californians worth over $1B (residents as of Jan 1, 2026, even if they later leave), due 2027 with a 5-year installment option. Real estate and most retirement accounts are excluded. 90% of proceeds must go to health care (mainly Medi-Cal), the rest to education/food assistance. Revenue is exempt from the Gann spending limit and school-funding requirements, and the state has discretion over how and when to spend it.

**Key findings weighing on my decision:**

1. **The revenue claims are far from settled.** Proponents (the measure's authors at UC Berkeley) project ~$100B. The nonpartisan LAO says only "tens of billions" and "very hard to predict." A Nov 2026 NBER paper by Stanford/Hoover economists found 7 billionaires already left the state (removing ~30% of the tax base) and projects only ~$30B gross, with a possible net *loss* of up to ~$39B in present value from lost ongoing income taxes.

2. **One-time money for a recurring, back-loaded problem.** The federal OBBBA Medi-Cal cuts are real and severe — but the largest share of the cuts lands after 2030, long after this one-time revenue is spent. Even the emergency framing is structurally mismatched to this tool.

3. **Weak fiscal guardrails.** Gann-limit and school-funding exemptions plus broad legislative discretion and no dedicated oversight provisions are exactly the kind of design California voters have historically rejected.

4. **Real expansion pathway and legal risk.** The measure includes a two-thirds legislative amendment clause (drafters say it's limited; election-law experts split on how limited), it's the first US wealth tax with a retroactive residency anchor, it includes "expedited judicial review" anticipating challenges, and it can be nullified by Props 41/42 if they out-vote it.

5. **Who's on each side.** Pro: SEIU-UHW, Bernie Sanders, the state Democratic Party, Ro Khanna. Con: the state's major medical and hospital organizations (California Medical Association, Primary Care Association, Children's Hospital Association), teachers, firefighters, building trades, both gubernatorial candidates — plus billionaires funding the opposition (Sergey Brin alone has spent $57M+, which is fair to note as a conflict of interest).

6. **Polling:** Both of California's most reputable pollsters (PPIC 46/52, UC Berkeley IGS 42/50, late Oct) show it trailing.

The "yes" case is moral and the crisis is genuine, but a durable funding gap is better addressed by durable revenue (Prop 3, which polls ahead with majority support), while this measure pairs an uncertain, one-time windfall below its advertised figure with broad spending discretion, an amendment pathway, and real litigation risk.

**No.**

Proposition 40
Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers. Initiative Constitutional Amendment and Statute.
Analysis of Measure
Background
California Is Home to Many Billionaires. Several of the wealthiest people in the world live in California. Wealth is the value of all the things a person owns. Wealth is different from income, which is how much a person earns in a set period of time, like one year. A person's wealth typically is measured by their net worth. A person's net worth is the value of all the things they own, like stocks, businesses, or other investments, minus their debts. California is home to a few hundred people with net worth over $1 billion, often called billionaires. Many of these billionaires gained their wealth as executives or investors in California technology companies.
Health Care Is a Major Category of State Spending. The state and federal government spend over $200 billion per year on state health care programs. Most state health care spending is for Medi-Cal, the state's health insurance program for low-income people. State spending also supports public health programs, mental health care, and drug and alcohol treatment.
Proposal
Establishes One-Time Wealth Tax on Billionaires. Under Proposition 40, billionaires who were residents of California on January 1, 2026 would have to pay a one-time state tax equal to 5 percent of their net worth. The tax would be due in 2027. Taxpayers would have the option to spread the payments over five years but would have to pay more to do so. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.
Most of the Money Must Be Spent on Health Care. The state would decide how and when to spend the money from the wealth tax, but it would have to be spent on certain types of services. Ninety percent of the money would have to be spent on health care services for the public. The rest would have to be spent on education, food assistance, and administration of the wealth tax. Existing rules in the State Constitution that limit spending and require the state to spend a certain amount on schools and community colleges would not apply to this money.
Potential Interactions With Other Propositions
If Proposition 41 or 42 on this same ballot receive more "yes" votes than Proposition 40, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters. This is because the courts could find that Proposition 41 or 42 conflict with Proposition 40.
Fiscal Effects
Temporary State Revenue Increase From Wealth Tax. The state probably would collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax. This temporary increase in state tax collections would be spread across several years. Exactly when and how much the state would collect is very hard to predict for many reasons. For example, it is hard to know what actions billionaires would take to reduce the amount of tax they pay. Also, much of the wealth is based on stock prices, which are always changing.
Possible Ongoing Decrease in State Income Tax Revenues. California billionaires, like all those earning money in the state, currently pay state taxes on their annual income. Billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away. These responses probably would reduce state revenues by less than $1 billion per year. This could mean less money for the state's General Fund, which is the account that pays for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.
State Costs to Administer the Wealth Tax. The state would have costs to determine how much wealth tax is owed and to collect tax payments. These costs could be tens of millions of dollars per year for several years. These costs would be paid from the new wealth tax revenues.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
Temporary state revenue increase from a new wealth tax on billionaires. These wealth tax revenues probably would add up to tens of billions of dollars spread over several years.
Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in state income tax revenue collected from billionaires.

PROP
40
IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON CERTAIN TAXPAYERS. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 40
YES ON PROP. 40 TO TAX BILLIONAIRES
Trump’s “Big, Ugly Bill” slashed funding for healthcare in California to pay for more billionaire tax breaks, eliminating coverage for over a million Californians and doubling health insurance premiums for millions more. Vote YES on Prop. 40 to make billionaires finally pay their fair share in taxes and stop sticking the middle class with the bill.
FUND HEALTHCARE, NOT BILLIONAIRE TAX BREAKS
Prop. 40 makes approximately 200 California billionaires pay a modest, one-time tax on their global wealth to keep local hospitals and ERs open and healthcare affordable for millions of Californians.
It will raise about $100 billion to replace the funding Trump and his billionaire donors took from working people to line their pockets. The funds will go to life-saving medical care for seniors, veterans, and families. It will allow millions of Californians to keep their health insurance and not see their premiums skyrocket. It will prevent mass teacher layoffs in our public schools and keep children fed through food assistance programs.
BILLIONAIRES SHOULD PAY THEIR FAIR SHARE
You pay your taxes out of every paycheck, but billionaires pay much lower rates than working families. They insist on paying less, even as they get bigger and bigger tax breaks.
Prop. 40 enacts a one-time tax paid ONLY by Californians worth more than $1 billion, a small group of people who together hold $2 trillion in wealth-most of which will never be taxed due to loopholes that favor the ultra-wealthy.
Billionaires amassed their extreme wealth on the backs of the middle class, and we have a chance to make them pay their fair share so WE aren’t stuck paying more for healthcare.
BERNIE SANDERS SUPPORTS PROP. 40
U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders strongly supports voting YES on Prop. 40, even if some politicians in Sacramento are protecting billionaires over working people.
“The idea that [billionaires] are saying it’s ok for children to die, for people not to get the healthcare they need, that they’re going to punish the people of California-it’s outrageous.”
-U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders.
DON’T BELIEVE THE BILLIONAIRES’ LIES
A small group of morally bankrupt billionaires is spreading lies about Prop. 40, because they want working people to foot the bill for their tax breaks.
Google founder and Trump donor Sergey Brin’s wealth has DOUBLED to nearly $300 billion since Trump’s election. Now he’s spent over $57 million to oppose Prop. 40. He’d rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay his fair share in taxes.
Billionaires like Brin have bought and paid for some corrupt politicians and organizational leaders to also oppose Prop. 40-but actual teachers, Planned Parenthood workers, nurses, and union members support it. Those opposing Prop. 40 have not put forth any viable solution to replacing the funding Trump took from us.
Of course these billionaires and their puppets don’t want a billionaire tax, but you should-because someone has to pay, and working people are already paying enough for healthcare.
SAVE LIVES. TAX BILLIONAIRES.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
Victoria Barron , Patient Access Specialist
Planned Parenthood of Pacific Southwest
Denise Robb , Ph.D., Member of American Federation of Teachers
Local 1521
Los Angeles College Faculty Guild
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 40
CALIFORNIA’S EDUCATION, HEALTHCARE, PUBLIC SAFETY, LABOR AND BUSINESS LEADERS ALL OPPOSE PROP. 40’s FLAWED TAX SCHEME
Prop. 40 is a flawed tax scheme that will damage our state while taxpayers pay the price.
Here’s why a broad coalition of California teachers, doctors, clinics, hospitals, firefighters, taxpayers, blue-collar labor unions, businesses, Democrats and Republicans oppose 40:
Prop. 40 won’t fill any funding gap-IT WILL COST CALIFORNIA $25 BILLION in lost revenue for schools, healthcare and public safety.
Prop. 40 won’t fix healthcare or lower costs for consumers-it’s a blank check that ALLOWS THE LEGISLATURE TO GIVE BILLIONS TO HEALTH INSURANCE COMPANIES, with no guarantees struggling families see a single cent to help them with high healthcare costs.
Prop. 40 won’t help schools: it exempts itself from California’s voter-approved protections for school funding. That SHORTCHANGES PUBLIC SCHOOLS $3 BILLION ANNUALLY.
Prop. 40 doesn’t solve inequality in California. It just pushes out the companies and successful residents who drive California’s economy, jobs and tax base-FORCING OTHER TAXPAYERS TO MAKE UP THE DIFFERENCE.
There’s more: the French economists and the lone group behind Prop. 40 knew the money from their flawed one-time tax would run out, so they included a loophole that lets the Legislature expand the tax without a vote of the people.
Prop. 40 has no accountability or oversight, and no safeguards to ensure the money is spent as intended.
California needs stable, accountable revenue to fund our schools, healthcare and public safety-NOT PROP. 40.
Get the facts and vote no on Prop. 40.
April O’Connor , Teacher
California Teachers Association
Rob Gutierrez , President
California Taxpayers Association (CalTax)
Chris Hannan , President
State Building and Construction Trades Council of California
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 40
No on 40-FLAWED WEALTH TAX “EXPERIMENT” HURTS ALL CALIFORNIANS
Prop. 40 is a poorly designed tax scheme that will damage our economy and cost our state budget billions of dollars-without doing anything to lower healthcare costs for Californians.
This measure is a one-time tax that only provides temporary funds. When the money runs out, the politicians will be back with yet another tax.
PROP. 40 WILL COST CALIFORNIA $25 BILLION IN LOST REVENUE FOR HEALTHCARE, EDUCATION
A study by Stanford University economists found the tax will cost California $25 billion as the tax drives companies and wealthy residents out-of-state.
These residents create new businesses, drive our economic growth and already pay nearly half the income taxes that fund state programs. If they leave, it will create a huge hole in our budget, threatening core services like education, healthcare and public safety or forcing other taxpayers to make up the difference.
California’s DOCTORS, HOSPITALS AND CLINICS OPPOSE PROP. 40 because the lost funding will endanger patients’ access to healthcare. “Prop. 40 doesn’t help the need for stable healthcare funding.
Prop. 40 makes it worse.”-Jodi Hicks, President and CEO, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California
PROP. 40 IS WRITTEN TO GIVE POLITICIANS NEW POWER TO EXPAND THE TAX
Prop. 40 isn’t just a “billionaire tax.” The special interests behind the measure wrote it to give the State Legislature power to amend the measure-without voter approval.
Independent legal analysis found Prop. 40 opens the door to expanding the tax to the assets of ALL Californians-to your savings, home equity and even retirement funds. www.ReadltForYourself.org
PROP. 40 TAXES RETIREMENT ACCOUNTS FOR THE FIRST TIME
Prop. 40 would be the first in California history to tax retirement accounts-a dangerous precedent. If it passes, it will inevitably be expanded to tax more Californians’ retirement savings.
PROP. 40 IS A RECIPE FOR MORE WASTEFUL SPENDING
State government spending is up 79% since 2019, without delivering better results on key issues like crime, housing and homelessness. But Prop. 40 includes no accountability, transparency or oversight provisions to ensure funds are spent as intended.
Instead, Prop. 40: • Exempts itself from voter-approved constitutional protections for schools, shortchanging classrooms over $3 billion annually. www.ProtectCaliforniaSchools.org • Exempts itself from the voter-approved state spending limit, including its requirement that excess revenues get returned to taxpayers. • Includes no safeguards to prevent billions from going directly to health insurance companies and CEOs.
AUTHORS ADMIT THE ONE-TIME TAX IS AN EXPERIMENT
The French economists who co-authored Prop. 40 have unsuccessfully proposed wealth taxes in France and the European Union that were rejected due to economic concerns. They call Prop. 40 “an experiment” that may backfire but say “California is the ideal place to test their idea.”
We shouldn’t risk California’s future on a costly economic experiment. www.WhoWroteProp40.org
PROP. 40 IS OPPOSED BY LABOR AND BUSINESS, DEMOCRATS AND REPUBLICANS, TEACHERS AND FIREFIGHTERS
Prop. 40 is opposed by Governor Gavin Newsom, the Democratic and Republican candidates for governor, and the following organizations: California Teachers Association, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, California Children’s Hospital Association, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, California Conference of Carpenters, California Professional Firefighters, California Asian Pacific Chamber of Commerce, California Council for Affordable Housing, California Taxpayers Association, California Chamber of Commerce, California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
Join us and vote no on this flawed tax scheme.
Visit www.VoteNoOn40.org for more information.
René Bravo , M.D., President
California Medical Association
Francisco Silva , CEO
California Primary Care Association
Dr. Debra Schade , President
California School Boards Association
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 40
LET’S CHECK THE FACTS
1. Prop. 40 is a BILLIONAIRE tax. It cannot be applied to anyone else-working people already pay more than their fair share.
2. Prop. 40 will GENERATE $100 billion to replace the healthcare funding Trump cut to fund billionaire tax breaks.
3. Billionaires pay MUCH LOWER TAX RATES compared to what working families pay out of every paycheck. DON’T LISTEN TO BILLIONAIRE LIES
The billionaires who helped Trump pass the “Big, Beautiful Bill” have spent millions to trick you into voting against a billionaire tax.
Don’t be fooled. The endorsements and studies from the billionaires are hiding the truth-they’re pushing a Trump agenda that protects billionaires and hurts everyday taxpayers.
ACTUAL DOCTORS, NURSES, TEACHERS, AND WORKERS SUPPORT PROP. 40
While some organizational leaders and lobbyists have sided with billionaires, the working people they’re supposed to represent are standing behind Prop. 40 and urging you to vote YES. Supporters include:
California Nurses Association, Representative Ro Khanna, Doctors with the Committee of Interns and Residents, SEIU, California League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC), Clergy and Laity United for Economic Justice (CLUE)
OPPONENTS OF PROP. 40 HAVE NO PLAN TO SAVE YOUR HEALTHCARE
The billionaires and their puppets have not put forth ANY viable solution to replacing the healthcare funding Trump took from us. They’d rather the middle class get stuck with shuttered hospitals and skyrocketing healthcare costs than pay their fair share.
Vote YES on Prop. 40.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
Victoria Barron , Patient Access Specialist
Planned Parenthood of Pacific Southwest
Denise Robb , Ph.D., Member of American Federation of Teachers
Local 1521
Los Angeles College Faculty Guild

This explainer was originally published by our news partners CalMatters. Be prepared for California’s midterms: Sign up for CalMatters' free election newsletter (https://calmatters.ac-page.com/california-elections-newsletter) and be the first to know when they update the CalMatters 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) with information on key races.
What does California Proposition 40 do?
Proposition 40 would require the estimated 200 Californians whose net worth exceeded $1 billion at the start of this year to pay a one-time 5% tax. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the group sponsoring the measure, projects that it would raise roughly $100 billion over five years. That money would be earmarked primarily for healthcare, with some reserved for food assistance and education. If propositions 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) or 42 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/) earn more votes than Proposition 40, this measure would be nullified.
Are you ready to vote? (https://www.kpbs.org/tags/elections)
California’s 2026 midterm elections will be held on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Get general information about the election, news coverage, an interactive ballot guide and results on election day.
Explore → (https://www.kpbs.org/tags/elections)
What do supporters and opponents say?
Supporters
Arguments for
Supporters argue that the people who would pay the tax are the ones who benefited the most financially from recent federal tax reforms. Congress also cut tens of billions from Medicaid, known as Medi-Cal in California, which provides health insurance to low-income people. SEIU-UHW argues those cuts will cause hospitals and clinics to close, costing thousands of jobs and worsening access for all patients.

Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders

Prop 40 guide: Why ‘yes’ or ‘no’ depends on two other California propositions
By Kathleen Pender (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/kathleen-pender/) , Contributor Updated Oct 31, 2026 1:33 p.m.
From left, California insurance commissioner candidate Jane Kim, Sen. Bernie Sanders, independent-Vt., and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., stand together onstage after the “Ballots Over Billionaires” wealth tax rally at the Curran Theatre in San Francisco.
Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle
Many Californians have strong opinions about Proposition 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-40-tax-billionaire-california-22477038.php), the proposed “wealth tax” on billionaires. But voting for — or against — this high-stakes ballot measure in November is not as simple as voting for — or against — Prop 40.
That’s because Props 41 and 42, which never mention billionaires but are backed by some of the state’s wealthiest residents, are also on the ballot and have provisions that conflict with Prop 40. (Props 41 and 42 do not conflict with each other.)

Under the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-10/), if two conflicting measures on the same ballot both pass with more than 50% of the vote, the one that gets the most “yes” votes prevails.
The graphic below shows the possible outcomes for which propositions could take effect, depending on how the votes come in. Voters can also use it to understand the cumulative impact of how they vote on each proposition.
What it means to vote ‘yes’ or ‘no’ on Props 40, 41 and 42
Prop 40, the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, would impose a one-time “wealth tax” on the net worth of people who were California residents as of Jan. 1, 2026 — even if they later became non-residents — and had more than $1 billion in net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. It also would exempt billionaire-tax revenues from three state-spending rules, including one known as the Gann limit.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 41 would conflict with Prop 40 because it would outlaw new taxes passed after Jan. 1, 2026 that are exempt from the Gann limit. Prop 42 also appears to counter Prop 40 by preventing new taxes on personal property (i.e., wealth) and taxes that apply retroactively, including those based on residency.
Backers of the billionaire tax are urging people (https://yeson40.com/) to vote “Yes” on 40 and “No” on Props 41 and 42. If voters follow that advice or, vote the exact opposite way, the outcomes would be straightforward:
If Prop 40 passes with more than 50% of the vote and Prop 41 and Prop 42 do not: The billionaire tax would take effect and the other two would not.
If Prop 40 loses and Prop 41 and/or 42 pass: The billionaire tax would fail. Prop 41 would take effect if it got a simple majority. So would Prop 42 if it passed.
But what happens if Prop 40 gets more than half the vote, and so does Prop 41 and/or 42? Here is the conventional wisdom:
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 41 passes with more votes than Prop 40: Prop 41 takes effect and the billionaire does not.
Prop 42 passes with more votes than Prop 40: Prop 42 takes effect, the billionaire tax dies.
Prop 40 passes with more votes than Prop 41: Prop 40 gets enacted, Prop 41 is invalidated.
Prop 40 passes with more votes than Prop 42: Prop 40 takes effect, and cancels out Prop 42.
Although these are likely scenarios, anything could happen in a court of law. The losing side could argue that its proposition doesn’t conflict with the winning one, so they should both take effect. A court would have to decide if they do conflict.
The losing side also might argue that some parts of its measure do not conflict with the winning proposition — and those parts should take effect. The California Supreme Court has rejected this piecemeal approach, but the issue could still wind up in litigation.
More importantly, any proposition declared the winner is almost sure to face legal challenges on its own merits. Anticipating such lawsuits, Prop 40 includes a procedure for “expedited judicial review of this act.”
Here’s a brief look at the measures, and how they conflict.

Article continues below this ad
Signs promote “yes” on Prop 40 and “no” on Props 41 and 42 before a rally at the Curran Theatre in San Francisco in early October.
Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle Proposition 40
Under Prop 40, most billionaires would owe a one-time 5% “excise” tax on net worth above $1.1 billion. The rate would be phased in between $1 billion and $1.1 billion.
The tax would apply to publicly traded securities, private-company stock, intellectual property and physical assets such as cars and artwork.
It would exclude homes, buildings and other real estate held directly by the taxpayer, as well as most retirement accounts. One exception: Roth IRA balances above $10 million would be taxed. Physical assets located outside California would also be excluded.
